messages.body_plain:
On Mar 8, 2010, at 14:50 , Ralf B wrote:

> When running a R script through the JRI interface using
>
> "source('" + scriptName + "')
>
> what is the best way to generally figure out if the script created an
> error or run error free?
>

try(source(myScriptFn), silent=TRUE)

and check for the class of the result -- if it's "try-error" then you  
have the error string, otherwise it's the result of the last statement  
in the script.

Cheers,
Simon

PS: I would recommend c.assign("fn", scriptPath);  
c.eval("source(fn)"); to avoid quoting hell ... pasting strings in  
Java as R commands is rather nasty.

> put all the matrix elements into an array and then do  
> c.eval(matrix(my_matrix))

That is correct, arrays are of the form double[] and that includes  
matrices in R. A matrix in R is an array with dim attributes, i.e.  
there is no double[][] in R (to be precise than would be a list of  
doubles - ie something like list(c(0.1,0.2,0.3),c(0.4,0.5,0.6))).

> an array of array from Java into R ?

Array (=type[]), yes. The is also the convenience method  
REXP.createDataFrame() where you create RList containing the columns.

> How exactly do I need to get an image or a plot from R to Java.
>

Please see PlotDemo.java in the examples. There are other ways, too,  
such as JavaGD.

Simon

You cannot instantiate JRI REngine more than once because R is not thread-safe and R shutdown implicitly closes the process (that is why end() doesn't really close R). You'll have to re-use the REngine instance that you first created or start a new Java process (or use Rserve if you want multiple R instances in parallel).

Just a brief word of warning - if you use rJava you should not be  
loading your classes via "the project" since that bypasses the rJava  
loader, but use .jaddClassPath() instead. In that case JavaGD also  
uses rJava to register itself and you can set JAVAGD_USE_RJAVA to tell  
JavaGD that it is ok to go straight to rJava.

However, if you add your project to the system class path, make sure  
you understand the consequences - your code won't be able to load or  
use classes from rJava and R packages implicitly since your classes  
(unlike all others) will be owned by the system class loader and not  
the rJava class loader. You can explicitly use the rJava class loader  
in your code, of course, and depending on what you do it may not be an  
issue.

The error you see comes probably from the fact that your classes  
attempt to load JavaGD via system loader which fails (when you add it  
to your "project" you register it with your system class loader so it  
disappears). JavaGD has a fall back for that situation to recover, but  
again - see above you should probably set JAVAGD_USE_RJAVA.

Cheers,
Simon
